**The saddest ten days**

Easter Monday, March 26, 1951

It must’ve been 10 o'clock in the morning when Dr Anne Casey, 36, hauled herself out of bed and waddled over to the mirror-image bedroom occupied by her husband, Dr Austie Casey, 52. As soon as she opened the door, she let out a yelp, to the horror of the children, because she had found him dead to the world. It was his third heart attack and he slipped away in his sleep, unable to recover from the festivities.

Anne had been sleeping in the other room because she was due to have the baby any day now, and the complications had already begun. There was still hope too. Laura had been a miracle and was a ruddy two year old now, the first Rhesus baby in Ireland to survive. She got the all-important blood transfusion that had only just become available. Austie must have had to muscle his way through his medical contacts in Dublin and managed to pull together a team who could save the baby. The chances of survival were lower for subsequent babies and Austie's clout would be needed to pull together the right team for this coming birth. Nine days later, the young widow would bear a still born baby, Joseph Patrick Casey, 0, and his little body would be buried beside his father in the loose soil of the family grave.

Jane was **five** and remembers it all. Richard was six and Michael, the eldest, was eight, his father's pride and joy, and now he would have to become the man of the house. It must have taken time for Anne to came to, then she called for help from the nanny. When no one came, Anne had to traipse downstairs, her flock trailing behind her, to ask the maids where that aul wan was gone to. They said she was gone to Mass. The aul dragon. She's always gone to mass when she's wanted. Anne struggled back up the stairs and Michael went in with his mammy to see his father, and him there, gone.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The early years had been idyllic for the Casey family. The war was over and the world was opening up. Michael Augustine Casey had long been the Medical Officer for the county town of Dungarvan in West Waterford, along the southern coast of Ireland. Incredibly, he was also the managing director of the town's two factories, both of which he had helped set up. In his latter years, he found himself and his beautiful wife travelling all around America, buying machines and visiting family in Chicago and Los Angeles. Business was booming now and the men of Dungarvan and surroundings areas had steady work, all year round, largely thanks to Austie Casey. Ireland in the 1950s hadn't happened yet and the mood was still good. No sooner were the lovers back from The States and they went on a cruise to Portugal and Madeira. They had a nanny and three maids to help them raise the children.

Soon the children would be like stray cats. With no father, their mother would be flat out as a dispensary doctor, working like a dog to keep the thing going, thanks to the paltry stipend she received in accordance with Austie's second will, which had been changed after one of his heart attacks. Soon enough, Austie's siblings all began to drop, some of them afflicted by the same heart condition. In ten years' time, only one of the six was still alive. **JOE?**

The following evening, Austie Casey's body lay **IN STATE i**n Mountain View, a sizeable home **that had been housing doctors for decades**. (MORE) That evening, the coffin would be removed to St Mary's Parish Church, **half a mile away,** by a relay of workers from the Glue and Gelatine factory which had been set up during the war by Austie and his younger brother Pierce. The inputs to the glue factory were bi-products of the tanning done in the Dickens Leather factory since 1935, when Austie Casey, with his tireless organizational skills, managed to convince the powers that be in Dublin that the perfect place for a tannery would be Dungarvan. The factory was set up in the very heart of the town, where the river meets the sea.

Funeral

The whole town was jammed on the Wednesday morning for the funeral and the car couldn't move through the crowd. The spacious church was full inside and hundreds had to stand in the precincts, but everyone could attend the burial immediately afterwards as the family plot was right by the entrance to the church. Present at the interment were Austie's surviving siblings, Fr Dick, Joe, Fr Rennie, Percy and May. It turns out that Austie would be buried beside his little brother, John, who was only a few years younger than Austie but who had died aged 11, in 1917. Joe, an accountant, would have flown all the way from Los Angeles, where Austie and Anne had visited him on their tour of the States. Dick would have surely driven from Skerries where he had, by his energetic standards, retired into a role as Parish Priest, a post he kept until his death in 1962. It is highly unlikely, given his profession, that he was at home for Easter when Austie died, although he certainly would become one the many regular guests in Mountain View. Rennie had come from Lancashire where he worked as part of a mission among the large Irish community, although he would see out his days in Mountain View, later that decade. Percy had stayed local although his galavanting days were about to begin as he would step into Austie's shoes before also succumbing to a heart attack. Percy also ran a shop in the middle of the town which had been owned by their father, Michael J., the much-loved champion of the town's poor, until his death in 1923, and later taken over by his wife, Catherine, until her death in 1940. The gathering for Austie was perhaps the largest in the town since his mother died.

## **Funeral**

Wednesday morning, 29 March, 1951

It's a **Wednesday** morning in late March and Dungarvan is dunta for the Doris Day. The busiest man in town has died and his funeral is today.

-   It's a curious irony that the now prosperous town has suspended business to celebrate the man who did more than anyone to bring work and wealth to the once-tough lives of people in a Free State town.

At his funeral today, it will be mentioned that Michael Augustine Casey, known as "Austie Casey", was "perhaps the greatest industrialist in Munster if not the country".

-   

    -   *with both first and second names together, like Tadgh Beirne or ...*

<!-- -->

-   It's a big claim as he may not have even been the greatest leatherman to grace County Waterford in the early twentieth century – that award surely goes to Limerick's Kennedy O'Brien, who helped established tanneries in both Portlaw and Dungarvan, and elsewhere too.

    -   That honour perhaps belongs to Kennedy O'Brien, a *bona fide* leather man, who lived and breathed leather production from the age of *seventeen* when he began working in ?1907? in Ireland's last remaining big tannery.

-   But that perhaps only demonstrates the culture of Free State Eire at a time when the colonial aristocrats had been recently ousted and the industrial heartlands of the northern province had been partitioned off, leaving the body of an island without its industrious legs.

    -   The country had to bootstrap itself into a functional economic entity, led by a small, educated middle-class who would scramble to fill the new power vacuum, and **powered** by a class of labourers who were capable of hard, physical, and even noxious work.

-   Austie's biggest strength was neither on the factory floor nor in the day-to-day running of the business. He was the one who brought jobs to the people of Dungarvan, and not just seasonal work, as would have been common, but year-round work for the people of the town and countryside.
